stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Planners in many mid-sized cities now test car-free streets on a small scale before making any permanent changes. One town closed its main market street to cars for a single summer. During those months, foot traffic on the street ______ several new cafés opened along its sidewalks.
explanation: Cover the blank and test each side. "During those months, foot traffic on the street doubled" can stand alone as a sentence. So can "several new cafés opened along its sidewalks." When both sides are sentences, a comma followed by a FANBOYS word such as "and" is a correct way to join them. This is the first check behind every run-on and comma-splice question on the test: before you look at the choices, decide whether each side is a full sentence.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. Both sides are complete sentences, and a comma alone cannot join them, even when the pause sounds natural out loud.

C.why: You ran two complete sentences together with no punctuation at all. Each one has its own subject and verb ("traffic doubled" and "cafés opened"), so they need a real join between them.

D.why: You had the right pieces in the wrong order. The comma belongs before "and", where the first sentence ends. A comma after "and" splits the conjunction off from the clause it introduces.

subtype_name: Run-on / comma splice: join or split two full sentences

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Music historians often learn the most from drafts that a composer chose not to publish. The composer Ilse Brandauer revised her only symphony four ______ in a private library, the first draft shows a slow movement nearly twice as long as the one in the final version.
explanation: "The composer Ilse Brandauer revised her only symphony four times" is a complete sentence. The words after the blank are a second complete sentence: the opening phrase "Surviving in a private library" describes "the first draft," which is the subject, and "shows" is its verb. When you have two sentences, a period separates them correctly. Learning to spot this lets you see through the participle trap that Hard boundary questions are built around.

B.why: You fell for the participle trap. "Surviving" makes the second half look like a phrase hanging off the first sentence, but "the first draft shows" completes it as its own sentence. The result is a comma splice.

C.why: You left out punctuation between two complete sentences. That creates a run-on, and it also makes it look as though the symphony was revised "surviving."

D.why: You used a semicolon and "and" together. A semicolon already joins two sentences without any help, so adding a FANBOYS word after it doubles the join and is not standard.

subtype_name: Run-on / comma splice: join or split two full sentences

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In relief printmaking, the image comes from what the artist leaves behind rather than from what the artist cuts. A woodcut printer carves away every part of the block that should stay ______ raised surface that remains is the only part that will hold ink.
explanation: "A woodcut printer carves away every part of the block that should stay white" can stand alone as a sentence. So can "the raised surface that remains is the only part that will hold ink." A semicolon is one of the three legal ways to join two complete sentences. On the real test, this is the same check you use whenever a semicolon appears among the choices: it needs a full sentence on both sides.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. The two ideas are closely related, but a comma alone still cannot join two complete sentences.

C.why: You ran the sentences together with no break. Without punctuation, "white the raised surface" reads as one unbroken phrase, which hides where the second sentence starts.

D.why: You treated "then" as if it were a joining word. It is not one of the FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so), so a comma followed by "then" is still a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Few marine mammals use tools, but the sea otter is a well-documented exception. Floating on its back, an otter opens clams and urchins by striking them against a stone balanced on its ______ single otter may keep the same favorite stone for weeks, tucking it into a loose pouch of skin under one foreleg.
explanation: "Floating on its back, an otter opens clams and urchins by striking them against a stone balanced on its chest" is a complete sentence. "A single otter may keep the same favorite stone for weeks" is another one, with its own subject ("otter") and verb ("may keep"). A period between two complete sentences is always correct. This is the base step for every run-on question: find where one complete thought ends and the next begins.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. A comma signals a pause, but a pause is not enough to separate two complete sentences.

C.why: You fused the two sentences with no punctuation, so "its chest a single otter" runs straight through the place where the first sentence ends.

D.why: You thought a transition word could do the joining. "However" is not a FANBOYS word, so with only commas around it, the two sentences still form a comma splice. A transition like this needs a period or a semicolon in front of it.
